I care not to perform this part of my task methodically; but shall be content to produce the desired impression by separate citations of items, practically or reliably known to me as a whaleman; and from these citations, I take it—the conclusion aimed at will naturally follow of itself.

First: I have personally known three instances where a whale, after receiving a harpoon, has effected a complete escape; and, after an interval (in one instance of three years), has been again struck by the same hand, and slain; when the two irons, both marked by the same private cypher, have been taken from the body. In the instance where three years intervened between the flinging of the two harpoons; and I think it may have been something more than that; the man who darted them happening, in the interval, to go in a trading ship on a voyage to Africa, went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and penetrated far into the interior, where he travelled for a period of nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, with all the other common perils incident to wandering in the heart of unknown regions. Meanwhile, the whale he had struck must also have been on its travels; no doubt it had thrice circumnavigated the globe, brushing with its flanks all the coasts of Africa; but to no purpose. This man and this whale again came together, and the one vanquished the other. I say I, myself, have known three instances similar to this; that is in two of them I saw the whales struck; and, upon the second attack, saw the two irons with the respective marks cut in them, afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so fell out that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time distinctly recognised a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale’s eye, which I had observed there three years previous. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here are three instances, then, which I personally know the truth of; but I have heard of many other instances from persons whose veracity in the matter there is no good ground to impeach.

Secondly: It is well known in the Sperm Whale Fishery, however ignorant the world ashore may be of it, that there have been several memorable historical instances where a particular whale in the ocean has been at distant times and places popularly cognisable. Why such a whale became thus marked was not altogether and originally owing to his bodily peculiarities as distinguished from other whales; for however peculiar in that respect any chance whale may be, they soon put an end to his peculiarities by killing him, and boiling him down into a peculiarly valuable oil. No: the reason was this: that from the fatal experiences of the fishery there hung a terrible prestige of perilousness about such a whale as there did about Rinaldo Rinaldini, insomuch that most fishermen were content to recognise him by merely touching their tarpaulins when he would be discovered lounging by them on the sea, without seeking to cultivate a more intimate acquaintance. Like some poor devils ashore that happen to know an irascible great man, they make distant unobtrusive salutations to him in the street, lest if they pursued the acquaintance further, they might receive a summary thump for their presumption.

But not only did each of these famous whales enjoy great individual celebrity—Nay, you may call it an ocean-wide renown; not only was he famous in life and now is immortal in forecastle stories after death, but he was admitted into all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name; had as much a name indeed as Cambyses or Cæsar. Was it not so, O Timor Tom! thou famed leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who so long did’st lurk in the Oriental straits of that name, whose spout was oft seen from the palmy beach of Ombay? Was it not so, O New Zealand Jack! thou terror of all cruisers that crossed their wakes in the vicinity of the Tattoo Land? Was it not so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose lofty jet they say at times assumed the semblance of a snow-white cross against the sky? Was it not so, O Don Miguel! thou Chilian whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics upon the back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to the students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classic scholar.

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times creating great havoc among the boats of different vessels, were finally gone in quest of, systematically hunted out, chased and killed by valiant whaling captains, who heaved up their anchors with that express object as much in view, as in setting out through the Narragansett Woods, Captain Butler of old had it in his mind to capture that notorious murderous savage Annawon, the headmost warrior of the Indian King Philip.

I do not know where I can find a better place than just here, to make mention of one or two other things, which to me seem important, as in printed form establishing in all respects the reasonableness of the whole story of the White Whale, more especially the catastrophe. For this is one of those disheartening instances where truth requires full as much bolstering as error. So ignorant are most landsmen of some of the plainest and most palpable wonders of the world, that without some hints touching the plain facts, historical and otherwise, of the fishery, they might scout at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.

First: Though most men have some vague flitting ideas of the general perils of the grand fishery, yet they have nothing like a fixed, vivid conception of those perils, and the frequency with which they recur. One reason perhaps is, that not one in fifty of the actual disasters and deaths by casualties in the fishery, ever finds a public record at home, however transient and immediately forgotten that record. Do you suppose that that poor fellow there, who this moment perhaps caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan—do you suppose that that poor fellow’s name will appear in the newspaper obituary you will read to-morrow at your breakfast? No: because the mails are very irregular between here and New Guinea. In fact, did you ever hear what might be called regular news direct or indirect from New Guinea? Yet I tell you that upon one particular voyage which I made to the Pacific, among many others we spoke thirty different ships, every one of which had had a death by a whale, some of them more than one, and three that had each lost a boat’s crew. For God’s sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! not a gallon you burn, but at least one drop of man’s blood was spilled for it.

Secondly: People ashore have indeed some indefinite idea that a whale is an enormous creature of enormous power; but I have ever found that when narrating to them some specific example of this two-fold enormousness, they have significantly complimented me upon my facetiousness; when, I declare upon my soul, I had no more idea of being facetious than Moses, when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

But fortunately the special point I here seek can be established upon testimony entirely independent of my own. That point is this: The Sperm Whale is in some cases sufficiently powerful, knowing, and judiciously malicious, as with direct aforethought to stave in, utterly destroy, and sink a large ship; and what is more, the Sperm Whale has done it.

First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Ere long, several of the whales were wounded; when, suddenly, a very large whale escaping from the boats, issued from the shoal, and bore directly down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he so stove her in, that in less than “ten minutes” she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the severest exposure, part of the crew reached the land in their boats. Being returned home at last, Captain Pollard once more sailed for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again upon unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and forthwith forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. At this day Captain Pollard is a resident of Nantucket. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have conversed with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.*

*The following are extracts from Chace’s narrative: “Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two several attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact manœuvres which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the shoal which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions, as if fired with revenge for their sufferings.” Again: “At all events, the whole circumstances taken together, all happening before my own eyes, and producing, at the time, impressions in my mind of decided, calculating mischief, on the part of the whale (many of which impressions I cannot now recall), induce me to be satisfied that I am correct in my opinion.”

Here are his reflections some time after quitting the ship, during a black night in an open boat, when almost despairing of reaching any hospitable shore. “The dark ocean and swelling waters were nothing; the fears of being swallowed up by some dreadful tempest, or dashed upon hidden rocks, with all the other ordinary subjects of fearful contemplation, seemed scarcely entitled to a moment’s thought; the dismal looking wreck, and the horrid aspect and revenge of the whale, wholly engrossed my reflections, until day again made its appearance.”
In another place—p. 45,—he speaks of “the mysterious and mortal attack of the animal.”

Secondly: The ship Union, also of Nantucket, was in the year 1807 totally lost off the Azores by a similar onset, but the authentic particulars of this catastrophe I have never chanced to encounter, though from the whale hunters I have now and then heard casual allusions to it.

Thirdly: Some eighteen or twenty years ago Commodore J——, then commanding an American sloop-of-war of the first class, happened to be dining with a party of whaling captains, on board a Nantucket ship in the harbor of Oahu, Sandwich Islands. Conversation turning upon whales, the Commodore was pleased to be sceptical touching the amazing strength ascribed to them by the professional gentlemen present. He peremptorily denied for example, that any whale could so smite his stout sloop-of-war as to cause her to leak so much as a thimbleful. Very good; but there is more coming. Some weeks after, the Commodore set sail in this impregnable craft for Valparaiso. But he was stopped on the way by a portly sperm whale, that begged a few moments’ confidential business with him. That business consisted in fetching the Commodore’s craft such a thwack, that with all his pumps going he made straight for the nearest port to heave down and repair. I am not superstitious, but I consider the Commodore’s interview with that whale as providential. Was not Saul of Tarsus converted from unbelief by a similar fright? I tell you, the sperm whale will stand no nonsense.

I will now refer you to Langsdorff’s Voyages for a little circumstance in point, peculiarly interesting to the writer hereof. Langsdorff, you must know by the way, was attached to the Russian Admiral Krusenstern’s famous Discovery Expedition in the beginning of the present century. Captain Langsdorff thus begins his seventeenth chapter:

“By the thirteenth of May our ship was ready to sail, and the next day we were out in the open sea, on our way to Ochotsh. The weather was very clear and fine, but so intolerably cold that we were obliged to keep on our fur clothing. For some days we had very little wind; it was not till the nineteenth that a brisk gale from the northwest sprang up. An uncommon large whale, the body of which was larger than the ship itself, lay almost at the surface of the water, but was not perceived by any one on board till the moment when the ship, which was in full sail, was almost upon him, so that it was impossible to prevent its striking against him. We were thus placed in the most imminent danger, as this gigantic creature, setting up its back, raised the ship three feet at least out of the water. The masts reeled, and the sails fell altogether, while we who were below all sprang instantly upon the deck, concluding that we had struck upon some rock; instead of this we saw the monster sailing off with the utmost gravity and solemnity. Captain D’Wolf applied immediately to the pumps to examine whether or not the vessel had received any damage from the shock, but we found that very happily it had escaped entirely uninjured.”

Now, the Captain D’Wolf here alluded to as commanding the ship in question, is a New Englander, who, after a long life of unusual adventures as a sea-captain, this day resides in the village of Dorchester near Boston. I have the honor of being a nephew of his. I have particularly questioned him concerning this passage in Langsdorff. He substantiates every word. The ship, however, was by no means a large one: a Russian craft built on the Siberian coast, and purchased by my uncle after bartering away the vessel in which he sailed from home.

In that up and down manly book of old-fashioned adventure, so full, too, of honest wonders—the voyage of Lionel Wafer, one of ancient Dampier’s old chums—I found a little matter set down so like that just quoted from Langsdorff, that I cannot forbear inserting it here for a corroborative example, if such be needed.

Lionel, it seems, was on his way to “John Ferdinando,” as he calls the modern Juan Fernandes. “In our way thither,” he says, “about four o’clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck against a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. * * * * * The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin!” Lionel then goes on to impute the shock to an earthquake, and seems to substantiate the imputation by stating that a great earthquake, somewhere about that time, did actually do great mischief along the Spanish land. But I should not much wonder if, in the darkness of that early hour of the morning, the shock was after all caused by an unseen whale vertically bumping the hull from beneath.

I might proceed with several more examples, one way or another known to me, of the great power and malice at times of the sperm whale. In more than one instance, he has been known, not only to chase the assailing boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself, and long withstand all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that head; and, as for his strength, let me say, that there have been examples where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship, and secured there; the whale towing her great hull through the water, as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that, if the sperm whale, once struck, is allowed time to rally, he then acts, not so often with blind rage, as with wilful, deliberate designs of destruction to his pursuers; nor is it without conveying some eloquent indication of his character, that upon being attacked he will frequently open his mouth, and retain it in that dread expansion for several consecutive minutes. But I must be content with only one more and a concluding illustration; a remarkable and most significant one, by which you will not fail to see, that not only is the most marvellous event in this book corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon—Verily there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth Christian century lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work every way of uncommon value. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unexaggerating historian, except in some one or two particulars, not at all affecting the matter presently to be mentioned.

Now, in this history of his, Procopius mentions that, during the term of his prefecture at Constantinople, a great sea-monster was captured in the neighboring Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after having destroyed vessels at intervals in those waters for a period of more than fifty years. A fact thus set down in substantial history cannot easily be gainsaid. Nor is there any reason it should be. Of what precise species this sea-monster was, is not mentioned. But as he destroyed ships, as well as for other reasons, he must have been a whale; and I am strongly inclined to think a sperm whale. And I will tell you why. For a long time I fancied that the sperm whale had been always unknown in the Mediterranean and the deep waters connecting with it. Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort. But further investigations have recently proved to me, that in modern times there have been isolated instances of the presence of the sperm whale in the Mediterranean. I am told, on good authority, that on the Barbary coast, a Commodore Davis of the British navy found the skeleton of a sperm whale. Now, as a vessel of war readily passes through the Dardanelles, hence a sperm whale could, by the same route, pass out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit is to be found, the aliment of the right whale. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale—squid or cuttle-fish—lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures, but by no means the largest of that sort, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together, and reason upon them a bit, you will clearly perceive that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius’s sea-monster, that for half a century stove the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

Lionel, it seems, was on his way to “John Ferdinando,” as he calls the modern Juan Fernandes. “In our way thither,” he says, “about four o’clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck against a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. * * * * * The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin!” Lionel then goes on to impute the shock to an earthquake, and seems to substantiate the imputation by stating that a great earthquake, somewhere about that time, did actually do great mischief along the Spanish land. But I should not much wonder if, in the darkness of that early hour of the morning, the shock was after all caused by an unseen whale vertically bumping the hull from beneath.

I might proceed with several more examples, one way or another known to me, of the great power and malice at times of the sperm whale. In more than one instance, he has been known, not only to chase the assailing boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself, and long withstand all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that head; and, as for his strength, let me say, that there have been examples where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship, and secured there; the whale towing her great hull through the water, as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that, if the sperm whale, once struck, is allowed time to rally, he then acts, not so often with blind rage, as with wilful, deliberate designs of destruction to his pursuers; nor is it without conveying some eloquent indication of his character, that upon being attacked he will frequently open his mouth, and retain it in that dread expansion for several consecutive minutes. But I must be content with only one more and a concluding illustration; a remarkable and most significant one, by which you will not fail to see, that not only is the most marvellous event in this book corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon—Verily there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth Christian century lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work every way of uncommon value. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unexaggerating historian, except in some one or two particulars, not at all affecting the matter presently to be mentioned.

Now, in this history of his, Procopius mentions that, during the term of his prefecture at Constantinople, a great sea-monster was captured in the neighboring Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after having destroyed vessels at intervals in those waters for a period of more than fifty years. A fact thus set down in substantial history cannot easily be gainsaid. Nor is there any reason it should be. Of what precise species this sea-monster was, is not mentioned. But as he destroyed ships, as well as for other reasons, he must have been a whale; and I am strongly inclined to think a sperm whale. And I will tell you why. For a long time I fancied that the sperm whale had been always unknown in the Mediterranean and the deep waters connecting with it. Even now I am certain that those seas are not, and perhaps never can be, in the present constitution of things, a place for his habitual gregarious resort. But further investigations have recently proved to me, that in modern times there have been isolated instances of the presence of the sperm whale in the Mediterranean. I am told, on good authority, that on the Barbary coast, a Commodore Davis of the British navy found the skeleton of a sperm whale. Now, as a vessel of war readily passes through the Dardanelles, hence a sperm whale could, by the same route, pass out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called _brit_ is to be found, the aliment of the right whale. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale—squid or cuttle-fish—lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures, but by no means the largest of that sort, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together, and reason upon them a bit, you will clearly perceive that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius’s sea-monster, that for half a century stove the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

modern_en.title: Chapter 45 — The Affidavit
paragraphs: As far as this book may have a narrative — and also because it indirectly touches on one or two very interesting and curious details of the habits of sperm whales — the foregoing chapter, in its earlier part, is as important as any to be found in this volume. But its leading matter needs to be enlarged upon still further, and more familiarly, in order to be properly understood, and also to remove any disbelief that a profound ignorance of the entire subject may produce in some minds as to the natural truth of the main points of this affair.

I do not care to do this part methodically, but will be content to make my point through separate examples of things practically or reliably known to me as a whaleman. From these examples, I trust, the conclusion I aim at will follow naturally.

First: I have personally known three instances where a whale, after receiving a harpoon, has made a complete escape and, after an interval (in one instance of three years), has been struck again by the same hand and killed — when the two irons, both marked with the same private cipher, have been taken from the body. In the instance where three years passed between the throwing of the two harpoons (and I think it may have been something more than that), the man who threw them happened in the interval to go in a trading ship on a voyage to Africa. He went ashore there, joined a discovery party, and made his way far into the interior, where he traveled for nearly two years, often endangered by serpents, savages, tigers, poisonous miasmas, and all the other common perils of wandering in the heart of unknown regions. Meanwhile the whale he had struck must also have been on its travels; no doubt it had circled the globe three times, brushing all the coasts of Africa with its flanks; but to no purpose. This man and this whale came together again, and the one vanquished the other. I say that I myself have known three instances like this: that is, in two of them I saw the whales struck, and after the second attack saw the two irons, with their respective marks cut in them, afterwards taken from the dead fish. In the three-year instance, it so happened that I was in the boat both times, first and last, and the last time I clearly recognized a peculiar sort of huge mole under the whale's eye which I had observed there three years before. I say three years, but I am pretty sure it was more than that. Here, then, are three instances whose truth I personally know; but I have heard of many other instances from people whose truthfulness in the matter there is no good reason to doubt.

Second: It is well known in the Sperm Whale Fishery, however ignorant the world ashore may be of it, that there have been several memorable historical cases where a particular whale in the ocean has been popularly recognizable at distant times and places. Why such a whale became marked in this way was not, entirely and originally, owing to bodily peculiarities distinguishing him from other whales; for however peculiar in that respect any chance whale may be, they soon put an end to his peculiarities by killing him and boiling him down into a peculiarly valuable oil. No: the reason was this — from the fatal experiences of the fishery, there hung about such a whale a terrible reputation for danger, as there did about the bandit Rinaldo Rinaldini, so much so that most fishermen were content to acknowledge him merely by touching their tarpaulin hats when they found him lounging near them on the sea, without trying to cultivate a closer acquaintance. Like some poor devils ashore who happen to know an irascible great man, they make distant, unobtrusive greetings to him in the street, for fear that if they pushed the acquaintance further they might get a summary thump for their presumption.

But each of these famous whales did more than enjoy great personal celebrity — no, call it ocean-wide renown; each was not only famous in life and immortal after death in forecastle stories, but was granted all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name, and had just as much of a name as Cambyses or Caesar. Wasn't it so, O Timor Tom! you famous leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who lurked so long in the Oriental straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palm-lined beach of Ombay? Wasn't it so, O New Zealand Jack! you terror of all the cruisers that crossed their wakes near the Tattoo Land? Wasn't it so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose tall jet, they say, sometimes took the shape of a snow-white cross against the sky? Wasn't it so, O Don Miguel! you Chilean whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics on your back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classical scholar.

But this is not all. New Zealand Tom and Don Miguel, after at various times causing great havoc among the boats of different ships, were finally hunted down, systematically pursued, and killed by valiant whaling captains who raised their anchors with that express purpose in mind — just as Captain Butler of old set out through the Narragansett Woods specifically to capture that notorious, murderous savage Annawon, the foremost warrior of the Indian King Philip.

I do not know where I can find a better place than right here to mention one or two other things which seem important to me, since in printed form they establish in all respects the reasonableness of the whole story of the White Whale, and especially of the catastrophe. For this is one of those disheartening cases where truth needs fully as much propping up as error. So ignorant are most landsmen of some of the plainest and most palpable wonders of the world that, without some hints about the plain facts, historical and otherwise, of the fishery, they might scoff at Moby Dick as a monstrous fable, or, still worse and more detestable, a hideous and intolerable allegory.

First: Though most men have some vague, flitting ideas of the general perils of the grand fishery, they have nothing like a fixed, vivid conception of those perils and of how often they recur. One reason, perhaps, is that not one in fifty of the actual disasters and accidental deaths in the fishery ever finds a public record at home, however brief and quickly forgotten that record may be. Do you suppose that that poor fellow there — who at this very moment, perhaps, caught by the whale-line off the coast of New Guinea, is being carried down to the bottom of the sea by the sounding leviathan — do you suppose that poor fellow's name will appear in the newspaper obituaries you will read tomorrow at breakfast? No: because the mails are very irregular between here and New Guinea. In fact, have you ever heard anything that could be called regular news, direct or indirect, from New Guinea? Yet I tell you that on one particular voyage I made to the Pacific, among many others we spoke — that is, hailed at sea — thirty different ships, every one of which had had a death by a whale, some of them more than one, and three that had each lost a boat's crew. For God's sake, be economical with your lamps and candles! There is not a gallon you burn that did not cost at least one drop of man's blood.

Second: People ashore have indeed some vague idea that a whale is an enormous creature of enormous power. But I have always found that when I have described to them some specific example of this twofold enormousness, they have pointedly complimented me on my facetiousness — when, I declare upon my soul, I was no more trying to be funny than Moses when he wrote the history of the plagues of Egypt.

But fortunately the particular point I am after here can be established on testimony entirely independent of my own. That point is this: the Sperm Whale is in some cases powerful enough, knowing enough, and judiciously malicious enough, with direct premeditation, to stave in, utterly destroy, and sink a large ship; and what is more, the Sperm Whale actually has done it.

First: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean. One day she saw spouts, lowered her boats, and gave chase to a shoal of sperm whales. Before long several of the whales were wounded, when suddenly a very large whale, escaping from the boats, broke out of the shoal and bore straight down upon the ship. Dashing his forehead against her hull, he stove her in so badly that in less than "ten minutes" she settled down and fell over. Not a surviving plank of her has been seen since. After the most severe exposure, part of the crew reached land in their boats. When he had at last returned home, Captain Pollard sailed once more for the Pacific in command of another ship, but the gods shipwrecked him again on unknown rocks and breakers; for the second time his ship was utterly lost, and, at once forswearing the sea, he has never tempted it since. Captain Pollard lives in Nantucket to this day. I have seen Owen Chace, who was chief mate of the Essex at the time of the tragedy; I have read his plain and faithful narrative; I have talked with his son; and all this within a few miles of the scene of the catastrophe.*

*The following are extracts from Chace's narrative: "Every fact seemed to warrant me in concluding that it was anything but chance which directed his operations; he made two separate attacks upon the ship, at a short interval between them, both of which, according to their direction, were calculated to do us the most injury, by being made ahead, and thereby combining the speed of the two objects for the shock; to effect which, the exact maneuvers which he made were necessary. His aspect was most horrible, and such as indicated resentment and fury. He came directly from the shoal which we had just before entered, and in which we had struck three of his companions, as if fired with revenge for their sufferings." Again: "At all events, the whole circumstances taken together, all happening before my own eyes, and producing, at the time, impressions in my mind of decided, calculating mischief on the part of the whale (many of which impressions I cannot now recall), induce me to be satisfied that I am correct in my opinion."

Here are his reflections some while after leaving the ship, on a black night in an open boat, when he had almost given up hope of reaching any friendly shore. "The dark ocean and swelling waters were nothing; the fears of being swallowed up by some dreadful tempest, or dashed upon hidden rocks, with all the other ordinary subjects of fearful contemplation, seemed scarcely entitled to a moment's thought; the dismal looking wreck, and the horrid aspect and revenge of the whale, wholly engrossed my reflections, until day again made its appearance."
In another place — page 45 — he speaks of "the mysterious and mortal attack of the animal."

Second: The ship Union, also of Nantucket, was totally lost off the Azores in 1807 by a similar attack, but the authentic details of this catastrophe I have never happened to encounter, though from whale hunters I have now and then heard passing references to it.

Third: Some eighteen or twenty years ago Commodore J——, then commanding an American sloop-of-war of the first class, happened to be dining with a party of whaling captains on board a Nantucket ship in the harbor of Oahu, Sandwich Islands. When the conversation turned to whales, the Commodore was pleased to be skeptical about the amazing strength attributed to them by the professional gentlemen present. He flatly denied, for example, that any whale could strike his stout sloop-of-war hard enough to make her leak so much as a thimbleful. Very good; but there is more to come. Some weeks later the Commodore set sail in this impregnable craft for Valparaiso. But he was stopped on the way by a portly sperm whale, who asked for a few moments of confidential business with him. That business consisted of giving the Commodore's craft such a thwack that, with all his pumps going, he made straight for the nearest port to heave her down — tip her on her side — and repair her. I am not superstitious, but I consider the Commodore's interview with that whale providential. Was not Saul of Tarsus converted from unbelief by a similar fright? I tell you, the sperm whale will stand no nonsense.

I will now refer you to Langsdorff's Voyages for a small detail particularly interesting to me. Langsdorff, you should know, was attached to the Russian Admiral Krusenstern's famous Discovery Expedition at the beginning of the current century. Captain Langsdorff begins his seventeenth chapter thus:

"By the thirteenth of May our ship was ready to sail, and the next day we were out in the open sea, on our way to Ochotsh. The weather was very clear and fine, but so intolerably cold that we were obliged to keep on our fur clothing. For some days we had very little wind; it was not till the nineteenth that a brisk gale from the northwest sprang up. An uncommon large whale, the body of which was larger than the ship itself, lay almost at the surface of the water, but was not perceived by any one on board till the moment when the ship, which was in full sail, was almost upon him, so that it was impossible to prevent its striking against him. We were thus placed in the most imminent danger, as this gigantic creature, setting up its back, raised the ship three feet at least out of the water. The masts reeled, and the sails fell altogether, while we who were below all sprang instantly upon the deck, concluding that we had struck upon some rock; instead of this we saw the monster sailing off with the utmost gravity and solemnity. Captain D'Wolf applied immediately to the pumps to examine whether or not the vessel had received any damage from the shock, but we found that very happily it had escaped entirely uninjured."

Now, the Captain D'Wolf referred to here as commanding the ship in question is a New Englander who, after a long life of unusual adventures as a sea-captain, now lives in the village of Dorchester near Boston. I have the honor of being his nephew. I have questioned him particularly about this passage in Langsdorff. He confirms every word. The ship, however, was by no means a large one: a Russian craft built on the Siberian coast, and bought by my uncle after he had bartered away the vessel in which he sailed from home.

In the voyage of Lionel Wafer, one of ancient Dampier's old chums — that straightforward, manly book of old-fashioned adventure, so full of honest wonders — I found a small incident set down so like what I just quoted from Langsdorff that I cannot resist inserting it here as a supporting example, if one is needed.

Lionel, it seems, was headed for "John Ferdinando," as he calls what is now Juan Fernández. "In our way thither," he says, "about four o'clock in the morning, when we were about one hundred and fifty leagues from the Main of America, our ship felt a terrible shock, which put our men in such consternation that they could hardly tell where they were or what to think; but every one began to prepare for death. And, indeed, the shock was so sudden and violent, that we took it for granted the ship had struck against a rock; but when the amazement was a little over, we cast the lead, and sounded, but found no ground. * * * * * The suddenness of the shock made the guns leap in their carriages, and several of the men were shaken out of their hammocks. Captain Davis, who lay with his head on a gun, was thrown out of his cabin!" Lionel goes on to blame the shock on an earthquake, and seems to back up that explanation by stating that a great earthquake at roughly that time really did cause great damage along the Spanish-held mainland. But I wouldn't be very surprised if, in the darkness of that early morning hour, the shock was actually caused by an unseen whale butting the hull straight up from below.

I might go on with several more examples, known to me one way or another, of the great power and malice the sperm whale at times shows. In more than one instance he has been known not only to chase the attacking boats back to their ships, but to pursue the ship itself and hold out for a long time against all the lances hurled at him from its decks. The English ship Pusie Hall can tell a story on that score; and as for his strength, let me say that there have been cases where the lines attached to a running sperm whale have, in a calm, been transferred to the ship and made fast there, the whale towing her great hull through the water as a horse walks off with a cart. Again, it is very often observed that if the sperm whale, once struck, is given time to rally, he then acts not so often with blind rage as with willful, deliberate designs of destruction against his pursuers; and it says something eloquent about his character that, when attacked, he will often open his mouth and hold it in that dreadful gape for several minutes on end. But I must be content with only one more, concluding illustration — a remarkable and most significant one, from which you will not fail to see not only that the most marvelous event in this book is corroborated by plain facts of the present day, but that these marvels (like all marvels) are mere repetitions of the ages; so that for the millionth time we say amen with Solomon — truly, there is nothing new under the sun.

In the sixth century of the Christian era lived Procopius, a Christian magistrate of Constantinople, in the days when Justinian was Emperor and Belisarius was general. As many know, he wrote the history of his own times, a work of uncommon value in every way. By the best authorities, he has always been considered a most trustworthy and unsensational historian, except in one or two particulars that do not affect the matter I am about to mention.

Now, Procopius reports in this history of his that while he was prefect of Constantinople, a great sea-monster was caught in the nearby Propontis, or Sea of Marmora, after it had been wrecking ships in those waters, off and on, for more than fifty years. A fact recorded like this in serious history is hard to dispute, and there is no reason anyone should want to. The account does not say exactly what species the monster was. But because it destroyed ships, and for other reasons too, it must have been a whale — and I lean strongly toward a sperm whale. Let me explain why. For a long time I assumed the sperm whale had never been known in the Mediterranean or in the deep waters that connect with it. Even now I am sure those seas are not, and perhaps under the present order of things never can be, a place where he regularly gathers in herds. But recent research has shown me that in modern times the sperm whale has turned up in the Mediterranean in isolated cases. I have it on good authority that a Commodore Davis of the British navy found a sperm whale's skeleton on the Barbary coast. And since a warship passes easily through the Dardanelles, a sperm whale could take the same route out of the Mediterranean into the Propontis.

In the Propontis, as far as I can learn, none of that peculiar substance called brit — the food of the right whale — is to be found. But I have every reason to believe that the food of the sperm whale — squid or cuttlefish — lurks at the bottom of that sea, because large creatures of that sort, though by no means the largest, have been found at its surface. If, then, you properly put these statements together and reason on them a bit, you will clearly see that, according to all human reasoning, Procopius's sea-monster, which for half a century stove in the ships of a Roman Emperor, must in all probability have been a sperm whale.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 45 — Den Sværgede Erklæring
paragraphs: Så vidt denne bog kan siges at have en handling — og også fordi det indirekte berører et par meget interessante og mærkelige enkeltheder om kaskelotternes vaner — er det foregående kapitel, i sin tidligere del, lige så vigtigt som noget andet i dette bind. Men dets hovedemne må udvides endnu mere og på en mere almindelig måde, for at blive rigtigt forstået, og også for at fjerne den vantro, som en dyb uvidenhed om hele emnet kan skabe hos nogle med hensyn til den naturlige sandhed i hovedpunkterne i denne sag.

Jeg har ikke lyst til at gøre denne del metodisk, men vil nøjes med at få mit synspunkt frem gennem enkeltstående eksempler på ting, som jeg som hvalfanger praktisk eller pålideligt kender. Ud fra disse eksempler vil den konklusion, jeg sigter mod, forhåbentlig følge naturligt.

For det første: Jeg har personligt kendt tre tilfælde, hvor en hval, efter at have fået en harpun i sig, er sluppet helt væk og efter et mellemrum (i det ene tilfælde på tre år) er blevet ramt igen af den samme hånd og dræbt — da de to jern, begge mærket med det samme private monogram, er blevet taget ud af kroppen. I det tilfælde, hvor der gik tre år mellem de to harpuners kast (og jeg tror, det kan have været noget mere end det), kom manden, der kastede dem, i mellemtiden til at tage med et handelsskib på en rejse til Afrika. Han gik i land dér, sluttede sig til et opdagelsesselskab og banede sig vej langt ind i det indre, hvor han rejste i næsten to år, ofte i fare for slanger, vildmænd, tigre, giftige uddunstninger og alle de andre almindelige farer ved at færdes i hjertet af ukendte egne. Imens må den hval, han havde ramt, også have været på sine rejser. Uden tvivl havde den sejlet rundt om kloden tre gange og strejfet hele Afrikas kyst med sine sider, men til ingen nytte. Denne mand og denne hval mødtes igen, og den ene overvandt den anden. Jeg siger, at jeg selv har kendt tre tilfælde som dette: det vil sige, at jeg i to af dem så hvalerne blive ramt, og efter det andet angreb så de to jern, med deres respektive mærker skåret ind, bagefter blive taget ud af den døde fisk. I treårstilfældet var jeg tilfældigvis med i båden begge gange, første og sidste gang, og den sidste gang genkendte jeg tydeligt en ejendommelig slags kæmpestort modermærke under hvalens øje, som jeg havde set dér tre år før. Jeg siger tre år, men jeg er ret sikker på, at det var mere end det. Her har vi altså tre tilfælde, hvis sandhed jeg personligt kender. Men jeg har hørt om mange andre tilfælde fra folk, hvis sandfærdighed i sagen der ikke er nogen god grund til at tvivle på.

For det andet: Det er velkendt i kaskelotfangsten, hvor uvidende verden på land end er om det, at der har været flere mindeværdige historiske tilfælde, hvor en bestemt hval i havet blev kendt af alle, til forskellige tider og på fjerne steder. Hvorfor en hval blev udpeget på den måde, skyldtes ikke helt og oprindeligt kropslige særtræk, der adskilte den fra andre hvaler. For hvor ejendommelig en tilfældig hval end er i den henseende, gør de snart ende på dens ejendommeligheder ved at dræbe den og koge den ned til en ejendommeligt værdifuld olie. Nej, grunden var denne: På grund af fangstens dødbringende erfaringer klæbede der til sådan en hval et frygteligt ry for farlighed, ligesom der gjorde om røveren Rinaldo Rinaldini. Så meget, at de fleste fangstfolk nøjedes med at hilse på den ved blot at røre ved deres tjærehatte, når de så den ligge og drive i nærheden af dem på havet, uden at forsøge at komme tættere på. Det er ligesom nogle stakkels stakler på land, der tilfældigvis kender en hidsig, stor mand: De hilser kort og tilbageholdende på ham på gaden af frygt for, at hvis de trængte sig længere ind på ham, kunne de få en øretæve på stedet for deres frækhed.

Men hver af disse berømte hvaler gjorde mere end at nyde stor personlig berømmelse — nej, kald det berømmelse over hele havet. Hver af dem var ikke blot berømt i live og udødelig efter sin død i historierne i mandskabsrummet, men fik et navns rettigheder, privilegier og værdighed og havde lige så meget af et navn som Cambyses eller Caesar. Var det ikke sådan, o Timor Tom! du berømte leviatan, arret som et isbjerg, du som så længe lurede i de østlige stræder, der bærer dit navn, og hvis sprøjt man ofte så fra den palmebevoksede strand ved Ombay? Var det ikke sådan, o New Zealand Jack! du skræk for alle krydsere, der krydsede dit kølvand ved Tattoo Land? Var det ikke sådan, o Morquan! Japans konge, hvis høje stråle, siges det, nogle gange tog form af et snehvidt kors mod himlen? Var det ikke sådan, o Don Miguel! du chilenske hval, mærket som en gammel skildpadde med hemmelighedsfulde hieroglyffer på ryggen! Med almindelige ord: Her er fire hvaler, der er lige så kendte for studerende af hvalernes historie som Marius eller Sylla for den klassiske lærde.

Men det er ikke det hele. New Zealand Tom og Don Miguel blev, efter at have gjort stor skade blandt bådene fra forskellige skibe ved forskellige lejligheder, til sidst jagtet ned, forfulgt systematisk og dræbt af tapre hvalfangerkaptajner, der lettede anker netop med det formål — ligesom kaptajn Butler i gamle dage drog ud gennem Narragansett-skovene for særligt at fange den berygtede, morderiske vilde Annawon, indianerkong Philips fornemste kriger.

Jeg ved ikke, hvor jeg kan finde et bedre sted end lige her til at nævne et par andre ting, som forekommer mig vigtige, eftersom de på tryk i alle henseender fastslår, at hele historien om den hvide hval, og især katastrofen, er rimelig. For det her er et af de nedslående tilfælde, hvor sandheden har lige så meget brug for støtte som vildfarelsen. De fleste landkrabber er så uvidende om nogle af verdens mest almindelige og håndgribelige undere, at de uden nogle vink om de nøgterne kendsgerninger, historiske og andre, ved fangsten kunne le af Moby Dick som en uhyrlig fabel eller, endnu værre og mere afskyeligt, en gruopvækkende og uudholdelig allegori.

For det første: Selv om de fleste mennesker har nogle vage, flygtige forestillinger om de store farer ved den store fangst, har de ikke noget, der ligner en fast, levende forestilling om disse farer og om, hvor ofte de gentager sig. En grund er måske, at ikke en ud af halvtreds af de virkelige ulykker og dødsfald i fangsten nogensinde bliver offentligt registreret herhjemme, hvor kort og hurtigt glemt den notits end måtte være. Tror du, at den stakkels fyr derude — som netop i dette øjeblik måske er fanget af hvallinen ud for New Guineas kyst og bliver slæbt ned til havets bund af den dykkende leviatan — tror du, at den stakkels fyrs navn vil stå i avisernes dødsannoncer, som du læser i morgen til morgenmaden? Nej, for posten er meget uregelmæssig mellem her og New Guinea. Ja, har du nogensinde hørt noget, man kunne kalde regelmæssige nyheder, direkte eller indirekte, fra New Guinea? Alligevel siger jeg dig, at jeg på en bestemt rejse til Stillehavet talte med — altså anråbte på havet — tredive forskellige skibe, blandt mange andre, og hvert eneste af dem havde haft en dødsulykke på grund af en hval, nogle af dem mere end én, og tre af dem havde hver mistet en hel bådbesætning. For Guds skyld, vær sparsommelig med dine lamper og lys! Der er ikke en gallon, du brænder, som ikke har kostet mindst én dråbe menneskeblod.

For det andet: Folk på land har rigtignok en vag forestilling om, at en hval er et enormt dyr med enorm kraft. Men jeg har altid oplevet, at når jeg har beskrevet et bestemt eksempel på denne dobbelte enormitet for dem, har de ligefrem rost mig for min vittighed — mens jeg, på min sjæl, ikke mere prøvede at være morsom end Moses, da han skrev historien om Egyptens plager.

Men heldigvis kan det særlige punkt, jeg er ude efter her, bevises ved vidnesbyrd, der er helt uafhængige af mit eget. Punktet er dette: Kaskelotten er i nogle tilfælde stærk nok, klog nok og velovervejet ondskabsfuld nok, med direkte forsæt, til at slå hul i, helt ødelægge og sænke et stort skib. Og hvad mere er, kaskelotten har faktisk gjort det.

For det første: I året 1820 krydsede skibet Essex, kaptajn Pollard, fra Nantucket i Stillehavet. En dag så hun sprøjt, sænkede sine både og gav jagt på en stime kaskelotter. Inden længe var flere af hvalerne såret, da en meget stor hval pludselig slap fra bådene, brød ud af stimen og gik lige ned mod skibet. Han slog panden mod hendes skrog og slog hende så slemt læk, at hun på under »ti minutter« sank sammen og kæntrede. Ikke en eneste af hendes planker er set siden. Efter de hårdeste strabadser nåede en del af besætningen land i bådene. Da kaptajn Pollard endelig var kommet hjem, sejlede han igen til Stillehavet som fører af et andet skib, men guderne lod ham forlise endnu en gang på ukendte skær og brydere. For anden gang gik hans skib fuldstændig tabt, og han svor straks havet fra sig og har aldrig fristet det siden. Kaptajn Pollard bor i Nantucket den dag i dag. Jeg har set Owen Chace, som var første styrmand på Essex på tidspunktet for tragedien. Jeg har læst hans enkle og pålidelige beretning. Jeg har talt med hans søn. Og alt det kun få engelske mil fra katastrofens skueplads.*

*Følgende er uddrag af Chaces beretning: »Alle kendsgerninger syntes at berettige mig til at slutte, at det var alt andet end tilfældighed, der styrede hans handlinger. Han angreb skibet to gange med kort mellemrum, og begge angreb var i deres retning beregnet til at gøre os størst mulig skade, idet de blev gjort forfra og dermed lagde de to tings fart sammen i stødet. For at opnå det var de nøjagtige manøvrer, han udførte, nødvendige. Hans udseende var forfærdeligt og viste vrede og raseri. Han kom direkte fra den stime, vi lige før var gået ind i, og hvor vi havde ramt tre af hans kammerater, som om han brændte af hævn for deres lidelser.« Igen: »Under alle omstændigheder får hele sammenhængen af omstændigheder, som alle skete for mine egne øjne og på det tidspunkt gav mig indtryk af afgjort, beregnende ondskab fra hvalens side (mange af disse indtryk kan jeg nu ikke genkalde mig), mig til at være tilfreds med, at min mening er rigtig.«

Her er hans overvejelser en tid efter, at han havde forladt skibet, en mørk nat i en åben båd, da han næsten havde opgivet håbet om at nå nogen venlig kyst. »Det mørke hav og de bølgende vande var ingenting. Frygten for at blive opslugt af en eller anden forfærdelig storm eller knust på skjulte skær, med alle de andre almindelige genstande for frygtsomme tanker, syntes næppe at fortjene et øjebliks eftertanke. Det dystre vrag og hvalens rædselsfulde udseende og hævn fyldte helt mine tanker, indtil dagen igen brød frem.«
Et andet sted — side 45 — taler han om »dyrets mystiske og dødbringende angreb«.

For det andet: Skibet Union, også fra Nantucket, gik fuldstændig tabt ud for Azorerne i 1807 ved et lignende angreb. Men de pålidelige enkeltheder om denne katastrofe er jeg aldrig tilfældigvis stødt på, selv om jeg nu og da har hørt hvalfangere nævne den i forbigående.

For det tredje: For en atten eller tyve år siden spiste kommandør J—— tilfældigvis til middag sammen med en flok hvalfangerkaptajner om bord på et skib fra Nantucket i havnen ved Oahu på Sandwich Islands. Han var dengang fører af et amerikansk krigsskib af første klasse. Da samtalen kom ind på hvaler, behagede kommandøren at være skeptisk over for den forbløffende styrke, som de tilstedeværende fagfolk tillagde dem. Han benægtede for eksempel blankt, at nogen hval kunne ramme hans solide krigsskib så hårdt, at hun ville lække så meget som et fingerbøl. Godt nok, men der er mere endnu. Nogle uger senere sejlede kommandøren af sted i dette uindtagelige fartøj mod Valparaiso. Men han blev standset undervejs af en velfødt kaskelot, som bad om et par øjeblikke til fortrolige forretninger med ham. Disse forretninger bestod i at give kommandørens fartøj sådan et dask, at han med alle pumper i gang sejlede lige til den nærmeste havn for at kølhale hende — lægge hende over på siden — og reparere hende. Jeg er ikke overtroisk, men jeg anser kommandørens samtale med den hval for et under af forsynet. Blev Saul af Tarsus ikke omvendt fra vantro ved et lignende chok? Jeg siger dig, kaskelotten finder sig ikke i noget sludder.

Jeg vil nu henvise dig til Langsdorffs rejseberetning for en lille enkelthed, som især interesserer mig. Langsdorff var, skal du vide, knyttet til den russiske admiral Krusensterns berømte opdagelsesekspedition i begyndelsen af det nuværende århundrede. Kaptajn Langsdorff begynder sit syttende kapitel sådan:

»Den trettende maj var vort skib klar til at sejle, og dagen efter var vi på åbent hav på vej til Ochotsh. Vejret var meget klart og dejligt, men så ulideligt koldt, at vi måtte beholde pelstøjet på. I nogle dage havde vi meget lidt vind. Først den nittende sprang der en kraftig kuling op fra nordvest. En usædvanlig stor hval, hvis krop var større end selve skibet, lå næsten i vandskorpen og blev ikke opdaget af nogen om bord, før i det øjeblik skibet, som gik for fulde sejl, næsten var oppe på den, så det var umuligt at undgå, at det stødte imod den. Vi blev dermed bragt i den største fare, for dette kæmpemæssige væsen løftede ved at rejse ryggen skibet mindst tre fod op af vandet. Masterne vaklede, og sejlene faldt alle sammen ned, mens vi, der var nede under dæk, alle straks sprang op på dækket i den tro, at vi var løbet på en klippe. I stedet så vi uhyret sejle bort med den største alvor og højtidelighed. Kaptajn D'Wolf satte straks pumperne i gang for at undersøge, om fartøjet havde taget skade af stødet, men vi fandt, at det heldigvis var sluppet helt uskadt.«

Nu er den kaptajn D'Wolf, der her nævnes som fører af det pågældende skib, en newenglænder, der efter et langt liv med usædvanlige eventyr som søkaptajn nu bor i landsbyen Dorchester nær Boston. Jeg har æren af at være hans nevø. Jeg har spurgt ham udførligt om netop denne passage hos Langsdorff. Han bekræfter hvert eneste ord. Skibet var dog på ingen måde stort: Det var et russisk fartøj bygget på den sibiriske kyst og købt af min onkel, efter at han havde byttet det skib væk, han var sejlet hjemmefra i.

I Lionel Wafers rejse — Wafer var en af gamle Dampiers gamle kammerater, og bogen er en ligefrem, mandig bog om gammeldags eventyr, så fuld af ærlige undere — fandt jeg en lille begivenhed beskrevet så nær ens med det, jeg lige har citeret fra Langsdorff, at jeg ikke kan lade være med at sætte den ind her som et støttende eksempel, hvis der er brug for et.

Lionel var, ser det ud til, på vej til »John Ferdinando«, som han kalder det, der nu hedder Juan Fernández. »På vejen derhen,« siger han, »omkring klokken fire om morgenen, da vi var omkring hundrede og halvtreds mil fra Amerikas fastland, fik vort skib et frygteligt stød, som bragte vore folk i sådan forfærdelse, at de næppe kunne sige, hvor de var, eller hvad de skulle tro. Men enhver begyndte at forberede sig på døden. Og stødet var i sandhed så pludseligt og voldsomt, at vi tog for givet, at skibet var løbet på en klippe. Men da forbløffelsen var lidt overstået, kastede vi loddet og pejlede, men fandt ingen bund. * * * * * Stødets pludselighed fik kanonerne til at springe i deres lavetter, og flere af mændene blev rystet ud af deres hængekøjer. Kaptajn Davis, som lå med hovedet på en kanon, blev kastet ud af sin kahyt!« Lionel går videre og skylder stødet på et jordskælv, og synes at støtte den forklaring ved at oplyse, at et stort jordskælv omtrent på det tidspunkt virkelig forvoldte stor skade langs det spanske fastland. Men jeg ville ikke blive særlig forbavset, hvis stødet i mørket på det tidlige morgentidspunkt i virkeligheden skyldtes en usynlig hval, der stødte skroget lige opad nedefra.

Jeg kunne fortsætte med flere eksempler, som jeg kender på den ene eller den anden måde, på den store kraft og ondskab, kaskelotten til tider viser. Mere end én gang har den ikke bare jagtet de angribende både tilbage til deres skibe, men forfulgt selve skibet og holdt stand i lang tid mod alle de lanser, der blev kastet mod den fra dækket. Det engelske skib Pusie Hall kan fortælle en historie om det. Og hvad dens styrke angår, så lad mig sige, at der har været tilfælde, hvor linerne fra en hval på flugt i vindstille blev ført over til skibet og gjort fast der, og hvalen slæbte hele det store skrog gennem vandet, som en hest går af sted med en vogn. Det bliver også meget ofte set, at hvis kaskelotten, når den først er ramt, får tid til at samle sig, handler den ikke så ofte i blind raseri som med bevidste, overlagte planer om at ødelægge sine forfølgere. Og det siger noget veltalende om dens karakter, at den, når den bliver angrebet, ofte åbner munden og holder den i det frygtelige gab i flere minutter i træk. Men jeg må nøjes med blot ét eksempel mere, til afslutning — et bemærkelsesværdigt og meget sigende et. Af det vil du ikke undgå at se, at ikke alene bliver den mest vidunderlige begivenhed i denne bog bekræftet af jævne kendsgerninger fra vor tid, men at disse undere (som alle undere) kun er gentagelser fra tidernes morgen. Så for en millionte gang siger vi amen sammen med Salomon — sandelig, der er intet nyt under solen.

I det sjette århundrede efter Kristi fødsel levede Procopius, en kristen dommer i Konstantinopel, i de dage da Justinian var kejser og Belisarius var feltherre. Som mange ved, skrev han sin egen tids historie, et værk af usædvanlig værdi i enhver henseende. Efter de bedste kilders mening har han altid været regnet for en højst troværdig og usensationel historiker, bortset fra et par enkeltheder, som ikke har betydning for det, jeg nu vil nævne.

Nu fortæller Procopius i denne sin historie, at mens han var præfekt i Konstantinopel, blev et stort havuhyre fanget i det nærliggende Propontis, eller Marmarahavet, efter at det med mellemrum havde ødelagt skibe i de farvande i mere end halvtreds år. Et faktum, der er optegnet sådan i alvorlig historieskrivning, er svært at bestride, og der er ingen grund til, at nogen skulle ønske det. Beretningen siger ikke præcis, hvilken art uhyret var. Men fordi det ødelagde skibe, og også af andre grunde, må det have været en hval — og jeg hælder stærkt til en kaskelot. Lad mig forklare hvorfor. I lang tid antog jeg, at kaskelotten aldrig var set i Middelhavet eller i de dybe farvande, der hænger sammen med det. Selv nu er jeg sikker på, at disse have ikke er, og måske under den nuværende orden aldrig kan blive, et sted hvor den regelmæssigt samles i flokke. Men nyere undersøgelser har vist mig, at kaskelotten i nyere tid er dukket op i Middelhavet i enkeltstående tilfælde. Jeg har det fra en god kilde, at en kommandør Davis fra den britiske flåde fandt et skelet af en kaskelot på Barbarikysten. Og da et krigsskib let kommer gennem Dardanellerne, kunne en kaskelot tage samme vej ud af Middelhavet ind i Propontis.

I Propontis findes, så vidt jeg kan finde ud af, intet af det ejendommelige stof, der kaldes brit — rethvalens føde. Men jeg har al mulig grund til at tro, at kaskelottens føde — blæksprutter eller sepier — lurer på bunden af det hav, fordi store væsner af den slags, dog på ingen måde de største, er fundet ved dets overflade. Hvis man så sætter disse udsagn ordentligt sammen og tænker lidt over dem, vil man klart se, at Procopius' havuhyre, som i et halvt århundrede slog hul i en romersk kejsers skibe, efter al menneskelig fornuft med al sandsynlighed må have været en kaskelot.
